claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the stability and integrity of a multi-element passive film.
The relevant multi-element passive film forms preferentially along grain boundaries.
A stable grain-boundary passive film minimizes mechanical damage.
A stable grain-boundary passive film minimizes electrochemical attack.
The target alloy has a uniform, multi-principal-element microstructure.
The target alloy develops a stable passive film under mild conditions.
The proposed baseline can be compositionally and microstructurally matched while having reduced passive-film stability at grain boundaries.
Under tribocorrosion, the grain-boundary passive film acts as a mechanical barrier that limits wear-induced material removal.
Under tribocorrosion, the grain-boundary passive film acts as a chemical barrier that reduces corrosion-driving electrochemical activity.
The film's combined mechanical and chemical protection delays the initiation and propagation of degradation-accelerating defects.
The target alloy will have lower total material loss than the less-passivating baseline under matched tribocorrosion conditions.
The target alloy's wear contribution to degradation will be lower than that of the baseline.
The target alloy's corrosion contribution to degradation will be lower than that of the baseline.
Combined degradation of the target alloy will be significantly lower than the additive wear and corrosion effects measured separately in the baseline.
The prediction should hold when wear does not continuously and completely remove the passive film.
The prediction should hold in corrosive environments where the passive-film chemistry remains effective.
The hypothesized protection may fail when extreme mechanical forces prevent passive-film persistence or reformation.
The hypothesized protection may fail when highly aggressive media prevent passive-film stability or reformation.
